messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When his colleague Tom fell from the scaffolding that afternoon, David saw everything — the sudden emptiness where a body had been, the sound that came after, the way the concrete turned dark. He was the one who called 911, but later he could never say what he had said. The memory refused to order itself: fragments of the morning briefing, the smell of diesel and metal, the nausea that rose as he looked down, Tom’s hard hat still spinning on the ground. Even now, fourteen months later, David finds himself unable to put the sequence straight in his head, and when he tries to describe it to his wife or the company counselor, the words vanish. He knows what happened, but there is a wall between the knowing and the saying. And then there are the moments when it is not a memory at all — when a sudden smell of diesel from a passing truck brings the scene back so vividly that he is there again, his hands shaking, the nausea rising, the violence of the fall replaying behind his eyes.

As an architect, David spends most of his days in a glass-walled office downtown, but he also visits construction sites to inspect progress. The first time he went back, three weeks after the accident, the foreman’s radio crackled and he flinched so hard he nearly dropped his clipboard. Now he knows the pattern: any reminder of what he saw — violence on a television screen, the smell of diesel or concrete dust, even the faint nausea that comes with a stomach bug — immediately floods him with hypervigilance. His heart speeds up, he scans the room for exits, and he positions himself so that his back is against a wall, where he can see everyone. He has come to believe that this vigilance is the only thing keeping him safe, because the world feels fundamentally dangerous and he is certain that he cannot stop bad things from happening. That helplessness was cemented the day he watched Tom fall and could do nothing. But it goes deeper: David is haunted by the conviction that there is something about him — some flaw, some unnoticed lapse — that made the accident happen. He was standing too close, he should have shouted a warning, he should have seen the loose guardrail. These thoughts intrude whenever he catches a whiff of diesel or hears a sudden shout, magnifying the trigger into a full-blown threat response. The more he monitors for danger, the more he notices potential threats — a cluttered hallway, an unsecured ladder, a colleague’s loud laugh — and each one drags him back into the memory again, the reliving so intense that he loses track of where he is. The cycle is self-reinforcing: a trigger provokes a memory, the memory spikes his threat level, and the heightened vigilance makes him more sensitive to the very cues that started it all.

David has withdrawn from the friendships he used to value. He feels isolated and set apart from his colleagues, who no longer understand why he asks to move desks so he can face the door, or why he excuses himself from team lunches in the noisy cafeteria. He never told them about his belief that he somehow caused the accident — that idea feels too shameful to voice — but it sits underneath everything, coloring his interactions and making him certain that others would blame him too. At home, his wife Sara has grown frustrated with his constant scanning of restaurant interiors and his refusal to visit the construction supply store where the smell of treated lumber reminds him of that afternoon. He knows his avoidance alarms her, but he cannot stop. What brought him to therapy was a moment three weeks ago in a department store: the scent of a cleaning product, the sudden reliving, and his uncontrolled urge to push through the emergency exit. A security guard stopped him, and Sara was in tears. David is afraid that next time he will hurt someone, or that the memories will swallow him whole. He hopes — though he can barely admit it — that there is a way to loosen the grip of what he saw, so he can walk through a room without measuring every wall and every door.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals cause or lead to triggers; instead, triggers evoke negative appraisals, and appraisals only magnify the threat response.
